title: Promotion tactics against weeks of no promotion

brief.decision: A take-home task from our hiring team in the Netherlands, on a public dataset, dunnhumby's Breakfast at the Frat: for each of its four categories, how average units per product, store and week under each promotion tactic compare with weeks of no promotion, to choose which tactic to study first. We ask for a difference, not the effect of a promotion.

expected_output.grain: one row per category and promotion tactic, weeks of no promotion left out

checkpoints.prompt: Ruben compares promotion tactics with weeks of no promotion in Breakfast at the Frat. Each sales row is one product in one store for one week, with three flags that are each 0 or 1: feature (in the weekly circular), display (on an in-store display) and tpr_only (a price reduction with no feature and no display). Which rows are weeks of no promotion?

options.text: Rows whose shelf price equals the base price, whatever the three flags say.
Rows with tpr_only 0, since a feature or a display costs the shopper nothing.
Rows with feature 0 and display 0, since a price reduction alone is not a promotion.
Rows with feature, display and tpr_only all 0, whatever the shelf price is.

checkpoints.prompt: In Breakfast at the Frat's sales, each row is one product in one store for one week, with three promotion flags that are each 0 or 1: feature, display and tpr_only. Across every week in the data, from the week ending 14 January 2009 to the week ending 4 January 2012, how many rows have two or more of the three flags set to 1? Type a whole number.
Write the query that answers Ruben's question.

In Breakfast at the Frat, take the products in the COLD CEREAL category, across every week from the week ending 14 January 2009 to the week ending 4 January 2012. Each sales row is one product in one store for one week. A row is a price reduction only when tpr_only is 1 and feature and display are both 0, and a week of no promotion when feature, display and tpr_only are all 0, whatever the price. Work out the average units per row in each of the two groups. By what percentage is the price-reduction-only average above the no-promotion average, that is 100 times (the first average minus the second) divided by the second? Type the percentage rounded to 1 decimal, for example 12.5.

In Ruben's table from Breakfast at the Frat, bag snacks sold far more units per product, store and week in display-only weeks than in weeks of no promotion, while price-reduction-only weeks sold about the same as weeks of no promotion. Nothing else has been checked yet. Ruben asks: can we conclude that displays work for bag snacks and price reductions do not?

options.text: Not yet. Tactics were not given at random, so the gap is a difference, not the effect; first compare the same product in the same store with and without each tactic.
Yes. Display weeks sold far more units than weeks of no promotion, so the display caused the extra units, and the price reductions caused none.
Yes. The table covers 156 weeks and thousands of rows for each tactic, which is enough data to rule out chance, so the gap is the effect.
No. A price reduction lowers the price, so only spend, not units, compares the tactics fairly; the same table in dollars would settle it.

checkpoints.prompt: Write 2 to 4 sentences for Ruben: which tactic shows the largest difference in each category, the cold cereal figure for a price reduction alone, one caveat about what the comparison cannot show, and one next step.

model_plan:
Metric formula: per category and tactic, product_store_weeks counts the sales rows and avg_units averages their units; no_promo_avg_units averages units over the category's rows of no promotion; units_diff_pct is 100 times (avg_units minus no_promo_avg_units) divided by no_promo_avg_units, rounded to 1 decimal.
Output grain: one row per category and tactic, weeks of no promotion left out.
Tables and keys: transactions joined to products on upc for the category; the store list is not needed.
Filters: every week from the week ending 14 January 2009 to the week ending 4 January 2012; each row classed as feature and display, feature only, display only, price reduction only or no promotion, checked in that order.
Edge cases: a row with tpr_only 1 that is also featured or on display takes its class from feature and display; a missing price does not change a row's class; the difference stays missing for a category with no week of no promotion.
Expected row count: 16
model_answer_template: In every category, weeks that were both featured and on display show the largest difference in average units against weeks of no promotion, and in cold cereal a price reduction alone still sold {CP4} percent more units per product, store and week. These are differences, not effects: tactics were not given to stores and products at random, and bag snacks show almost no difference for a price reduction alone. Before the budget is set, I would compare the same product in the same store with and without each tactic, and check the weeks just after each promotion.
follow_up_question: Can we conclude that displays work for bag snacks and price reductions do not?

data_source.label: Nearly real data: dunnhumby's Breakfast at the Frat, 156 weeks of store sales and promotions for products in four categories. Source: dunnhumby. Licence: dunnhumby terms, for research, personal or non-commercial use.
